subject: Air Navigation
question: Compass deviation is the angle between
explanation: Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north, produced by magnetic influences within the aircraft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Aircraft Magnetism and the Compasses'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A constant deviation on every heading is normally represented by which coefficient'
explanation: Coefficient A is the constant term and commonly represents a displaced lubber line or detector alignment error.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Aircraft Magnetism and the Compasses'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Earth convergency is best defined as
options: the distance between two meridians along a parallel
the angle of inclination between selected meridians at a stated latitude
half the difference between two rhumb-line tracks
the angle between true and magnetic north
explanation: Earth convergency is the angle of inclination between two selected meridians measured at a stated latitude.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Convergency and Conversion Angle'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Two meridians are 40 degrees apart at latitude 30 degrees north. Their convergency is
explanation: Convergency = 40 × sin 30 degrees = 20 degrees.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Convergency and Conversion Angle'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities
question: The direction in which the longitudinal axis of an aircraft points is its
explanation: Heading is the direction in which the aircraft's longitudinal axis points.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities
question: The direction of the path actually followed over the Earth's surface is the
explanation: Track is the direction of the aircraft's actual path over the Earth's surface.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities'

subject: Air Navigation
question: What is departure in navigation'
options: The angular difference between two meridians
The east-west distance between meridians along a stated parallel
The shortest great-circle distance between two positions
explanation: Departure is the east-west distance between two meridians measured along a specified parallel of latitude.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Departure'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Two meridians differ by 20 degrees at latitude 52 degrees. What is the departure'
explanation: Departure = 1,200 minutes × cos 52 degrees = 738.8 NM, which is about 739 NM.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Departure'

subject: Air Navigation
question: In the red and blue pole convention, the Earth behaves as if which polarity lies in the northern magnetic region'
explanation: The northern magnetic region behaves as a blue polarity, which attracts the red north-seeking end of a compass magnet.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Earth Magnetism'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Magnetic variation is the angle between
options: the horizontal and the total magnetic field
explanation: Variation is the horizontal angle between true north and magnetic north at a stated place and time.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Earth Magnetism'

subject: Air Navigation
question: In chart projection, the reduced Earth is
options: the area omitted from a chart
a scale model of the Earth used as the projection basis
the part of the globe below the equator
explanation: The reduced Earth is the scale model of the globe on which the projection is based.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'General Chart Properties'

subject: Air Navigation
question: The three general developable projection surfaces are
explanation: The three general families use a plane, a cylinder or a cone as the developable surface.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'General Chart Properties'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Which description defines a great circle'
options: Any circle drawn on the Earth's surface
A surface circle whose plane passes through the Earth's centre
A route that keeps a constant direction
explanation: A great circle has the same centre and radius as the Earth because its plane passes through the Earth's centre.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Great Circles and Rhumb Lines'

subject: Air Navigation
question: What is the defining property of a rhumb line'
options: It always passes through both poles
It is always the shortest surface route
It cuts every meridian at the same angle
explanation: A rhumb line cuts every meridian at the same angle, which makes it a line of constant direction.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Great Circles and Rhumb Lines'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Two checkpoints are 20 NM apart and elapsed time is 8 minutes. Measured groundspeed is
explanation: Groundspeed is 20 multiplied by 60 divided by 8, which gives 150 kt.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'In-flight Navigation Technique'

subject: Air Navigation
question: An aircraft passes A at 1010 and B, 30 NM farther, at 1027. If 20 NM remains, revised ETA is approximately
explanation: The measured 30 NM took 17 minutes, so the remaining 20 NM takes about 11 minutes and ETA is about 1038.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'In-flight Navigation Technique'

subject: Air Navigation
question: The principal navigation advantages sought in a Lambert conformal chart are
options: straight rhumb lines and true area
constant scale at every point and straight meridians
a visible geographic pole and equal area
near constant scale and nearly straight great-circle routes
explanation: Lambert was designed to give near constant scale and make a straight chart line a close approximation to a great circle.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Lambert's Conformal Chart: Part 1'

subject: Air Navigation
question: On a simple conic projection, scale is correct at
explanation: The simple cone touches the reduced Earth at its parallel of tangency, so scale is correct there.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Lambert's Conformal Chart: Part 1'

subject: Air Navigation
question: For practical aviation use, a chart may be treated as constant scale when its scale distortion does not exceed about
explanation: A Lambert sheet is treated as practically constant scale when its distortion remains within about 1 percent.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Lambert's Conformal Chart: Part 2'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A Lambert chart whose standard parallels are 16 degrees apart has an approximate maximum scale error of
explanation: Oxford's guide gives about 1 percent maximum scale error for 16 degrees of standard-parallel separation.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Lambert's Conformal Chart: Part 2'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A normal Mercator chart is correctly described as
explanation: The normal Mercator is cylindrical, mathematically modified and conformal, so it is non-perspective.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Mercator Charts: Properties'

subject: Air Navigation
question: The graticule of a direct Mercator chart is
explanation: Parallel straight meridians and parallel straight latitudes form a rectangular Mercator graticule.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Mercator Charts: Properties'

subject: Air Navigation
question: The scale at latitude L on a normal Mercator is
options: equatorial scale multiplied by sec L
equatorial scale multiplied by cos L
equatorial scale divided by tan L
explanation: Mercator scale at latitude L is the equatorial scale multiplied by secant L.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Mercator Charts: Scale'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A Mercator has scale 1:1,000,000 at the equator. Its scale at 60 degrees north is
explanation: Secant 60 degrees is 2, so the scale doubles and the RF becomes 1:500,000.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Mercator Charts: Scale'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP
question: Two aircraft 460 NM apart fly directly towards each other at groundspeeds of 250 kt and 210 kt. Their closing speed is
explanation: For head-on motion the groundspeeds add, giving a closing speed of 460 kt.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP
question: An aircraft at 220 kt is 80 NM behind traffic at 180 kt on the same track. Time to overtake is
explanation: Relative closing speed is 40 kt, so 80 NM divided by 40 kt gives 2 hours.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP'

subject: Air Navigation
question: An aircraft is 4 NM left of track after 30 NM. Its approximate track error is
explanation: Track error is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 30, which gives 8 degrees left.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Navigation Using the 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A 78 NM leg has 30 NM gone and a fix 4 NM left of track. What is the closing angle to destination'
explanation: Distance to go is 48 NM, so closing angle is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 48, or 5 degrees.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Navigation Using the 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule
question: At 2 NM on a 3.5 degree glidepath, the approximate height above the touchdown reference is
explanation: Height is 100 multiplied by 3.5 multiplied by 2, which gives 700 ft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule
question: At 4 NM on a 2.6 degree glidepath, the approximate height is
explanation: Height is 100 multiplied by 2.6 multiplied by 4, which gives 1040 ft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
question: A position line is best described as
options: a line somewhere along which the aircraft is known to be at a stated time
the line joining two planned waypoints
explanation: A position line is a line somewhere along which the aircraft is known to be at the observation time.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Plotting'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Fixes at 1700 and 1730 are 100 NM apart. The measured groundspeed is
explanation: One hundred nautical miles in 30 minutes is 200 kt.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Plotting'

subject: Air Navigation
question: For a North Polar stereographic chart, the plane touches the North Pole and the projection point is at
explanation: A North Polar stereographic is projected from the diametrically opposite South Pole onto a plane tangent at the North Pole.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Polar Stereographic and Grid Navigation'

subject: Air Navigation
question: The co-latitude of 70 degrees north is
explanation: Co-latitude equals 90 minus latitude, so 90 minus 70 gives 20 degrees.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Polar Stereographic and Grid Navigation'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Chart scale is the relationship between
options: a chart length and the corresponding Earth distance
explanation: Scale relates a measured chart length to the corresponding distance between the same positions on Earth.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Scale'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Which set gives the three common methods of expressing scale'
options: Statement in words, graduated scale line, representative fraction
explanation: Scale is commonly expressed by a word statement, a graduated scale line or a representative fraction.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Scale'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude
question: Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter subscale is set to
explanation: Pressure altitude is read with the standard pressure setting of 1013.25 hPa on the subscale.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude
question: Calibrated airspeed is obtained by correcting IAS for
explanation: CAS is IAS corrected for position or pressure error; the aircraft card may combine this with instrument correction.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude'

subject: Air Navigation
question: After 60 NM an aircraft is 7 NM left of planned track. Its track error is approximately
explanation: At the 60 NM reference distance, 7 NM off represents approximately 7 degrees left.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'The 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
question: After travelling 120 NM from an on-track fix, an aircraft is 8 NM right of track. The track error is
explanation: Sixty multiplied by 8 divided by 120 gives a track error of 4 degrees right.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'The 1 in 60 Rule'

subject: Air Navigation
question: For navigation calculations, what is the Earth's approximate compression'
explanation: The working compression is about 0.3 per cent, which is approximately 1 in 300; Bali gives the more exact ratio near 1 in 297.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'The Earth, Direction and Position'

subject: Air Navigation
question: What does the term graticule describe'
options: Every line printed on a chart
The network of meridians and parallels on a globe, map or chart
Only the small circles near a pole
explanation: The graticule is the network formed by meridians and parallels, including the prime meridian and equator as its reference lines.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'The Earth, Direction and Position'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Time 1: The Solar System and Time
question: The measurement of a day is based primarily on Earth's
explanation: A day is defined from Earth's rotation measured against the Sun or a distant star.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 1: The Solar System and Time'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Time 1: The Solar System and Time
question: Perihelion normally occurs in
explanation: Earth is nearest the Sun at perihelion in early January.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 1: The Solar System and Time'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line
question: An arc of 153 degrees 30 minutes is equivalent to approximately
explanation: At 15 degrees per hour, 153 degrees 30 minutes converts to 10 hours 14 minutes.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line'

subject: Air Navigation
topic: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line
question: To find LMT from UTC at an easterly longitude, the longitude expressed as time is
options: always rounded to a whole hour
explanation: East longitude is ahead of UTC, so its arc time is added to UTC to obtain LMT.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line'

subject: Air Navigation
question: On 21 June, the lowest listed northerly latitude at which the Sun remains above the horizon all day is
explanation: The Air Almanac question gives 66 degrees north as the lowest listed latitude with continuous daylight on 21 June.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 3: Sunrise, Sunset and Twilight'

subject: Air Navigation
question: On 21 December, the lowest listed northerly latitude at which the Sun does not rise is
explanation: The Air Almanac question gives 68 degrees north as the lowest listed latitude at which the Sun does not rise on 21 December.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Time 3: Sunrise, Sunset and Twilight'

subject: Air Navigation
question: Which of these chart scales normally gives the greater ground detail'
explanation: The 1:500,000 chart is the larger scale among these choices and normally shows more ground detail.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Topographical Maps and Map Reading'

subject: Air Navigation
question: On a contour chart, very closely spaced contours indicate
explanation: A steep slope produces a large elevation change over a short horizontal distance, so its contours lie close together.
source: R.K. Bali Air Navigation / Oxford ATPL Gen Nav, Chapter 'Topographical Maps and Map Reading'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which surveillance system can detect a reflecting aircraft without an airborne transponder'
explanation: PSR detects reflected radio energy and therefore does not require an airborne transponder.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'ATS Surveillance'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What determines when ADS-C sends a normal surveillance report'
options: The terms and triggers in the ground-held contract
A broadcast request from every nearby aircraft
The rotation rate of a radar antenna
explanation: ADS-C reports according to the periodic, event or demand conditions defined in its ground-held contract.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'ATS Surveillance'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the sole objective of an Annex 13 safety investigation'
options: To prevent future accidents and incidents
explanation: The sole objective is prevention of future accidents and incidents, not apportionment of blame or liability.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Accident Investigation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: When does an injury count as fatal under Bali's national accident definition'
options: When it causes death within 30 days of the accident
explanation: Bali treats an accident injury as fatal when death occurs within 30 days of the accident date.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Accident Investigation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which working position normally controls traffic on the manoeuvring area except runways'
explanation: The ground controller normally controls manoeuvring-area traffic except the runways.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodrome Control'

subject: Air Regulations
question: During low-visibility procedures, how should vehicle and person movements on the manoeuvring area be managed'
options: They are restricted to the essential minimum and ILS sensitive areas are protected
explanation: Low-visibility procedures restrict persons and vehicles to the essential minimum and protect ILS critical and sensitive areas.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodrome Control'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What display identifies a land-aerodrome identification beacon'
explanation: A land-aerodrome identification beacon flashes green characters in International Morse Code.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodromes: Lighting and Services'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What distinguishes the inner 300 m of a precision category II or III approach-light system'
options: White centre-line barrettes with red side-row barrettes
explanation: The inner 300 m is strengthened by white centre-line barrettes and red side-row barrettes.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodromes: Lighting and Services'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which area includes the manoeuvring area and aprons'
explanation: The movement area includes the manoeuvring area, aprons and relevant aircraft-maintenance movement areas.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodromes: Markings'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What determines aerodrome reference-code element 2'
options: Wingspan and outer main gear wheel span
explanation: Element 2 is the letter determined from wingspan and outer main gear wheel span.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aerodromes: Markings'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which ICAO Annex contains the Standards and Recommended Practices for aeronautical information services'
explanation: Annex 15 contains the Standards and Recommended Practices for aeronautical information services.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aeronautical Information'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which product is primarily used for a permanent change to AIP content'
explanation: An AIP amendment is the controlled product for a permanent change to AIP content.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Aeronautical Information'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which ATS objective is served by notifying rescue organisations about an aircraft needing aid'
options: The search and rescue support objective
explanation: Notifying and assisting the organisations responsible for search and rescue is one of the five ATS objectives.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Airspace and ATS'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which airspace structure begins at the surface and protects arriving and departing controlled flights'
explanation: A control zone begins at the surface and contains the relevant arriving and departing flight paths.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Airspace and ATS'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which ICAO Annex contains the international airworthiness Standards'
explanation: Annex 8 contains the international Standards for the airworthiness of aircraft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Airworthiness'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which State determines whether an aircraft on its register continues to be airworthy'
explanation: The State of Registry determines whether an aircraft on its register continues to be airworthy.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Airworthiness'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which setting makes an altimeter indicate altitude above mean sea level'
explanation: QNH makes the altimeter indicate altitude referenced to mean sea level.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Altimeter Setting'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What should a correctly set QFE altimeter indicate at its reference datum'
explanation: QFE is the pressure at the stated datum, so the altimeter indicates zero there.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Altimeter Setting'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which instrument is the principal current Indian statute in the hierarchy described in this chapter'
explanation: Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam 2024 is the principal current Indian statute, while the Rules and Civil Aviation Requirements provide more detailed requirements.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Definitions and Framework'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which Indian authority has the core civil aviation security oversight role'
explanation: BCAS is the authority responsible for civil aviation security policy, standards and oversight.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Definitions and Framework'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the main purpose of Annex 9 facilitation'
options: To expedite international air transport while maintaining necessary controls
To replace customs with airline staff
explanation: Annex 9 expedites aircraft, people and goods while preserving necessary customs, immigration, health, security and law-enforcement controls.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Facilitation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What happens when an aircraft-clearance document has been accepted electronically'
options: The same document should not also be demanded on paper
It may be ignored by authorities
It must always be sent twice
explanation: Once authorities accept the required electronic document, they should not demand the identical document again on paper.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Facilitation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which Chicago Convention Article establishes complete and exclusive State sovereignty over the airspace above its territory'
explanation: Article 1 establishes complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above a State's territory.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'ICAO and Conventions'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What does Article 6 require before a scheduled international air service operates over or into another State'
options: Special permission or authorisation from that State
explanation: Special permission or authorisation from that State is required for a scheduled international air service under Article 6.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'ICAO and Conventions'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which law replaced the Aircraft Act, 1934 as India's principal civil aviation enabling statute'
explanation: The Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024 replaced the Aircraft Act, 1934 as the principal enabling statute.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Indian Regulatory System'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which body has the central role of investigating aircraft accidents and incidents in India'
explanation: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau is the body responsible for investigating aircraft accidents and incidents.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Indian Regulatory System'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which threshold IAS places an aeroplane in Category C'
explanation: Category C covers a threshold IAS from 121 to 140 kt.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Instrument Approaches and Holding'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which segment normally connects the en-route phase to the IAF'
explanation: The arrival segment connects the en-route structure or STAR to the IAF.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Instrument Approaches and Holding'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Where is full MOC provided in a track-guided protected area'
explanation: Full MOC applies across the primary area; in each secondary area it tapers to zero at the outer edge.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Instrument Departures'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What engine condition is assumed in the design of a published instrument departure'
explanation: PANS-OPS departure procedures assume all engines are operating, so the operator develops the engine-out contingency.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Instrument Departures'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which ICAO Annex contains the Standards for aircraft nationality and registration marks'
explanation: Annex 7 contains the international Standards for Aircraft Nationality and Registration Marks.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Nationality and Registration'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Who assigns the individual registration mark to an aircraft'
options: The State of Registry or common mark registering authority
explanation: The State of Registry or common mark registering authority assigns the aircraft's registration mark.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Nationality and Registration'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the relationship between an operator's MEL and the approved MMEL'
options: The MEL replaces all Flight Manual limits
The MMEL applies only to one flight
The MEL cannot be less restrictive than the MMEL
explanation: The operator's approved MEL is tailored from, and cannot be less restrictive than, the approved MMEL.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Operational Hazards'

subject: Air Regulations
question: When does holdover time begin'
options: At the start of the final de-icing or anti-icing application
At the end of the first inspection
explanation: Holdover time begins at the start of the final de-icing or anti-icing application.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Operational Hazards'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What does an AOC or permit authorise'
explanation: An AOC or permit authorises the operator to conduct specified commercial air transport operations.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Operational Procedures'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which item belongs in the operational-manual group carried on board'
explanation: The Minimum Equipment List is one of the operational documents carried for the flight.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Operational Procedures'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the minimum age stated by Bali for an aeroplane CPL'
explanation: The minimum age for an aeroplane Commercial Pilot's Licence is 18 years.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Personnel Licensing'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which language level is Operational and must be re-evaluated every three years'
explanation: Level 4 is Operational, is accepted, and requires re-evaluation every three years.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Personnel Licensing'

subject: Air Regulations
question: When may the pilot-in-command depart from a Rule of the Air'
options: Only when absolutely necessary in the interests of safety
explanation: A pilot-in-command may depart from a Rule only when circumstances make it absolutely necessary in the interests of safety.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Rules of the Air: General'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What must pre-flight action include for an IFR flight'
options: Current weather, fuel requirements and an alternative course of action
explanation: IFR pre-flight action includes current weather information, fuel requirements and an alternative course of action if the plan cannot be completed.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Rules of the Air: General'

subject: Air Regulations
topic: Rules of the Air: VFR, IFR and Signals
question: What flight visibility is required at or above 10,000 ft AMSL under the standard VMC table'
explanation: The standard VMC minimum at or above 10,000 ft AMSL is 8 km flight visibility.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Rules of the Air: VFR, IFR and Signals'

subject: Air Regulations
topic: Rules of the Air: VFR, IFR and Signals
question: Which statement describes a Special VFR flight'
options: It may ignore ATC in a control zone
It is an IFR flight in visual conditions
It is individually cleared within a control zone and remains clear of cloud with the surface in sight
It is available above FL 150 without approval
explanation: Special VFR is an individually cleared control-zone operation that remains clear of cloud and in sight of the surface.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Rules of the Air: VFR, IFR and Signals'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which unit coordinates search and rescue operations throughout one SAR region'
explanation: The Rescue Coordination Centre organises SAR service and coordinates operations throughout its SAR region.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Search and Rescue'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which organisation coordinates maritime SAR policy in Bali's Indian framework'
options: The National Maritime Search and Rescue Board
explanation: The National Maritime Search and Rescue Board coordinates maritime SAR policy under the Indian Coast Guard leadership described by Bali.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Search and Rescue'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the primary objective of Annex 17 security measures'
options: Safety of passengers, crew, ground personnel and the public
explanation: The safety of passengers, crew, ground personnel and the public is the primary Annex 17 objective.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Security'

subject: Air Regulations
question: Which body is India's specialist civil aviation security regulator and oversight authority'
explanation: The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security, BCAS, sets standards and oversees civil aviation security in India.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Security'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What is the normal vertical separation minimum below FL 290'
explanation: Below FL 290, the normal vertical separation minimum is 1,000 ft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Separation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: When does the Bali VOR divergence method establish lateral separation'
options: At 5 degrees with both aircraft overhead
At 30 degrees with no distance condition
At 15 degrees with at least one aircraft 15 NM from the facility
explanation: The VOR method uses at least 15 degrees divergence with one aircraft at least 15 NM from the facility.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Separation'

subject: Air Regulations
question: When may a one-minute interval be used between two departures under Bali's stated divergence case'
options: Only when vertical separation already exists
Whenever the preceding aircraft is faster
When both aircraft fly the same SID
When their tracks diverge by at least 45 degrees immediately after take-off
explanation: One minute applies when the departure tracks diverge by at least 45 degrees immediately after take-off.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Separation Near Aerodromes'

subject: Air Regulations
question: What speed relationship supports Bali's two-minute same-track departure interval'
options: The following aircraft is at least 20 kt faster
The preceding aircraft is at least 40 kt faster
Both aircraft have identical filed speeds
The preceding aircraft is at least 10 kt faster
explanation: The two-minute same-track case requires the preceding aircraft to be 40 kt or more faster than the following aircraft.
source: R.K. Bali Air Regulations / ICAO Annexes, Chapter 'Separation Near Aerodromes'

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which almost all weather phenomena occur, is called the:
explanation: The troposphere extends from the surface to about 16-18 km at the equator and 8-10 km at the poles. It contains about 75% of the atmospheric mass and virtually all weather phenomena.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 1 'Atmosphere', Page 5

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), what is the standard temperature and pressure at mean sea level'
explanation: ICAO ISA specifies sea level temperature as +15°C (288.15 K), pressure as 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg), and density as 1225 g/m³ with a lapse rate of 6.5°C/km (approx 1.98°C/1000 ft) up to 11 km.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 1 'Atmosphere', Page 7

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The height of the tropopause is:
options: Constant over all latitudes at 11 km
Highest at the equator (16-18 km) and lowest at the poles (8-10 km)
Highest at the poles and lowest at the equator
Dependent only on the time of day
explanation: Due to intense solar heating and strong vertical convective currents in the tropics, the tropopause reaches 16-18 km at the equator, while over the cold poles it lies between 8-10 km.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 1 'Atmosphere', Page 5

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In ISA, from 11 km to 20 km altitude, the temperature is assumed to:
explanation: In the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, temperature decreases at 6.5°C/km from sea level to 11 km (-56.5°C), and then remains isothermal at -56.5°C from 11 km up to 20 km.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 1 'Atmosphere', Page 7

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Roughly, a 1 hPa decrease in atmospheric pressure near mean sea level corresponds to an increase in height of approximately:
explanation: Near mean sea level, 1 hPa change in pressure corresponds to approximately 27 to 30 ft (96 * T/P ft). At 20,000 ft it is about 50 ft/hPa, and at 40,000 ft about 100 ft/hPa.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 2 'Atmospheric Pressure', Page 12

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: When flying from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure without resetting the altimeter subscale, the altimeter will:
options: Read correctly because pitot-static tube compensates
Fluctuate rapidly between high and low readings
explanation: Rule: 'High to Low, Look Out Below'. When flying from high to low pressure, the altimeter senses lower pressure and interprets it as higher altitude, thus over-reading. The true altitude is lower than indicated.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 2 'Atmospheric Pressure', Page 19

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Which pressure setting is defined as the aerodrome station level pressure reduced to mean sea level assuming ISA conditions'
explanation: QNH is station pressure reduced to MSL using ISA temperature lapse rate. When set on the altimeter subscale on the ground, the altimeter reads aerodrome elevation above MSL.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 2 'Atmospheric Pressure', Page 18

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In the standard atmosphere, the 500 hPa and 300 hPa pressure levels correspond approximately to which altitudes'
explanation: Standard isobaric levels in ISA: 850 hPa = 5,000 ft (FL50); 700 hPa = 10,000 ft (FL100); 500 hPa = 18,000 ft (FL180); 300 hPa = 30,000 ft (FL300); 200 hPa = 38,000 ft (FL380).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 2 'Atmospheric Pressure', Page 19 Table 2.1

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: On a clear day with calm winds, the minimum surface air temperature normally occurs:
options: Half an hour to one hour after sunrise
Exactly at the moment of sunrise
explanation: Due to nocturnal radiational cooling, ground temperatures continue falling after sunrise until incoming solar radiation balances outgoing terrestrial radiation, typically 30 to 60 minutes after dawn.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 3 'Temperature', Page 32

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected back into space by clouds, aerosols, and the Earth surface is termed:
explanation: Albedo is the ratio of reflected solar radiation to total incident solar radiation. Earth's average albedo is about 30%, whereas fresh snow reflects about 80%.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 3 'Temperature', Page 31

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Density altitude is defined as:
options: The pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature
The altitude above ground level in standard temperature
The indicated altitude corrected for instrument error
The true altitude minus terrain elevation
explanation: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. In aviation, high density altitude reduces aircraft performance: longer takeoff run, slower rate of climb, and reduced engine power.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 4 'Air Density', Page 36

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: For every 1°C increase in temperature above ISA, the density altitude increases by approximately:
explanation: A rule of thumb in aviation meteorology states that for each 1°C rise above standard ISA temperature, density altitude increases by approximately 120 ft above pressure altitude.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 4 'Air Density', Page 36

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The temperature to which moist air must be cooled at constant pressure to reach saturation is called the:
explanation: Dew point (Td) is the temperature to which unsaturated air must be cooled at constant pressure and moisture content to become saturated (100% relative humidity).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 5 'Humidity', Page 41

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: When unsaturated air is lifted adiabatically, what happens to its Relative Humidity (RH) and Dew Point (DP)'
options: RH increases and DP decreases (by approx 2°C/km)
RH and DP both remain unchanged
RH increases while the humidity mixing ratio increases
explanation: As air rises, it expands and cools at DALR (9.8°C/km). Dew point falls at approx 1.8°C to 2°C/km. The temperature and dew point converge, so Relative Humidity increases until saturation (LCL).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 5 'Humidity', Page 41-42

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In the Northern Hemisphere, Buys Ballot's Law states that if an observer stands with their back to the wind:
options: Low pressure is to their right and high pressure to their left
Low pressure is to their left and high pressure to their right
explanation: Buys Ballot's Law states that in the Northern Hemisphere, an observer facing downwind has lower pressure to the left and higher pressure to the right. In the Southern Hemisphere, this is reversed.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 6 'Winds', Page 46

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Coriolis force is directly proportional to wind speed and the sine of latitude. Where is Coriolis force zero'
explanation: Coriolis force = 2 * omega * V * sin(phi). Since sin(0°) = 0, Coriolis force is zero at the Equator and reaches its maximum value at the poles where sin(90°) = 1.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 6 'Winds', Page 47

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: A cold, dense wind blowing down a mountain slope at night due to surface cooling is termed a:
explanation: Katabatic winds are gravity-driven down-slope winds caused by nocturnal radiational cooling of the mountain slopes, making the air heavier than surrounding free air.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 6 'Winds', Page 54

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: A sudden increase in wind speed of at least 16 kt (32 km/h), reaching 22 kt or more and lasting for at least one minute, is classified as a:
explanation: WMO defines a squall as a sudden increase of wind speed by at least 16 kt (8 m/s), the speed rising to 22 kt (11 m/s) or more and lasting for at least one minute. Gusts are transient fluctuations of seconds.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 6 'Winds', Page 46

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In aviation weather reports, 'Fog' (FG) is reported when the horizontal visibility is reduced by water droplets or ice crystals to less than:
explanation: By international aeronautical definition, fog is reported when visibility is less than 1000 m and relative humidity is near 100%. If visibility is between 1000 m and 5000 m with RH >= 95%, it is reported as Mist (BR).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 7 'Visibility and Fog', Page 66

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Radiation fog is most likely to form under which combination of meteorological conditions'
options: Strong winds (> 15 kt), overcast stratus sky, and dry air
Light winds (2-7 kt), clear skies at night, and high relative humidity
Calm wind, cloudy sky, and warm advection
Gale force winds and heavy precipitation
explanation: Radiation fog requires high relative humidity, clear skies for maximum terrestrial radiation cooling, and light wind (2-7 kt) to produce gentle turbulent mixing confined to a shallow layer near the ground.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 7 'Visibility and Fog', Page 69

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Advection fog forms when:
options: Cold dry air blows over warm land
Warm, moist air moves horizontally over a cold land or sea surface
Air is cooled adiabatically by climbing a mountain
Rain falls into cold surface air
explanation: Advection fog forms when warm moist air is transported over a colder underlying surface, cooling the air to its dew point. It can form over land or sea at any time of day or night and with moderate winds.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 7 'Visibility and Fog', Page 70

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Which cloud type is characterized by great vertical development, an anvil-shaped fibrous top, and hazards including severe turbulence, hail, and microbursts'
explanation: Cumulonimbus (CB) is the thunderstorm cloud. It features massive vertical development, anvil cirrus top, and poses the most severe hazards in aviation (turbulence, severe icing, wind shear, hail, lightning).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 8 'Clouds', Page 78

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Optical halos around the sun or moon are produced by light refraction through ice crystals in which cloud type'
explanation: Cirrostratus (CS) clouds consist of hexagonal ice crystals that refract sunlight or moonlight at a 22° angle, producing a circular halo with the red component on the inside.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 8 'Clouds', Page 77; Chapter 10 'Optical Phenomena', Page 94

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Precipitation consisting of very small, closely spaced water droplets (diameter < 0.5 mm) falling almost exclusively from Stratus cloud is termed:
explanation: Drizzle (DZ) consists of small water droplets of diameter 0.1 to 0.5 mm that appear to float in air currents. It falls almost exclusively from Stratus (ST) clouds.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 11 'Precipitation', Page 100

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Rain falling from a cloud that evaporates completely before reaching the ground is called:
explanation: Virga is precipitation falling from a cloud base that evaporates in dry air below before reaching the ground. It often indicates strong downdrafts beneath the cloud.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 11 'Precipitation', Page 101

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) and Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR) near sea level are approximately:
explanation: DALR is constant at 9.8°C/km (approx 3°C/1000 ft). SALR is lower because latent heat released during condensation warms the rising air, averaging about 5°C/km near sea level.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 9 'Stability and Instability', Page 86

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: If the Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR) is greater than the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR), the atmosphere is in a state of:
explanation: When ELR > DALR (super-adiabatic), lifted parcels of both dry and saturated air are warmer and less dense than the environment, continuing to accelerate upward (Absolute Instability).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 9 'Stability and Instability', Page 87

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Clear ice (glazed ice) on an airframe is most dangerous because it:
options: Is light and easily shaken off by vibration
Is heavy, transparent, adheres tenaciously, alters airfoil shape, and is hard to remove
Forms only on parked aircraft overnight
explanation: Clear ice forms from large supercooled water droplets at temperatures between 0°C and -10°C. The drops flow back before freezing, forming a dense, tenacious, transparent coating that severely degrades lift and adds weight.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 12 'Ice Accretion', Page 106

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Carburetor icing in piston engines is most likely to occur in which temperature and humidity conditions'
options: At ambient temperatures between -7°C and +30°C in moist air (RH > 60%)
Only when flying through heavy rain at 0°C
explanation: Fuel vaporization and adiabatic pressure reduction at the carburetor throttle butterfly can drop air temperature by up to 20°C. Carburetor ice can form even in warm ambient air up to +30°C with high relative humidity.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 12 'Ice Accretion', Page 107

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The mature stage of a thunderstorm lifecycle is definitively marked by:
options: The first appearance of an anvil top
The beginning of rain at the Earth's surface and the onset of downdrafts
The cessation of all lightning flashes
Weakening of the updrafts throughout the entire cell
explanation: The mature stage begins when falling precipitation reaches the surface. Rain drags cold air downward, generating downdrafts and the first gust / squall front. Updrafts and downdrafts coexist in this stage.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 13 'Thunderstorm', Page 113

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: A microburst is a localized intense downdraught with a horizontal diameter of less than 4 km. Its lifecycle typically lasts about:
explanation: Microbursts typically last 15 to 20 minutes. Peak winds develop 5 minutes after surface contact. An aircraft flying through encounters increasing headwind, strong downdraft, and then a dangerous sudden tailwind.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 13 'Thunderstorm', Page 117-118

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: What is the typical slope of a cold front compared to a warm front'
options: Cold front is flatter (1:150 to 1:180), warm front is steeper
Cold front is steeper (approx 1:50 to 1:80), warm front is shallower (approx 1:150 to 1:180)
Both fronts have the identical slope of 1:100
Cold fronts have no slope as they are vertical walls
explanation: Cold fronts advance like a blunt wedge with a steep slope of about 1:50 to 1:80, causing rapid vertical lifting and convective clouds (CU, CB). Warm fronts have a shallow slope of 1:150 to 1:180 with stratiform clouds.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 14 'Air Masses Fronts and Western Disturbances', Page 128-129

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Western Disturbances (WDs) affecting northern India during winter originate primarily over which region'
options: Mediterranean Sea and Caspian Sea region
explanation: Western Disturbances originate as extra-tropical low-pressure systems over the Mediterranean and Caspian Seas, travelling eastward steered by the Subtropical Westerly Jet stream into Pakistan and northern India.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 14 'Air Masses Fronts and Western Disturbances', Page 132

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: By WMO definition, the arbitrary lower speed limit for the core of a jet stream is:
explanation: WMO defines a jet stream as a strong narrow current of winds concentrated along a quasi-horizontal axis in the upper troposphere or stratosphere, with a minimum core speed of 60 kt (30 m/s).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 15 'Jet Streams', Page 136

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The Subtropical Jet Stream (STJ) affects northern India primarily during which months'
options: October to May (winter and transition seasons)
explanation: The Subtropical Westerly Jet Stream prevails over northern India from October to May, reaching peak core speeds of 100-150 kt in January/February near 27° N at 12 km (200 hPa).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 15 'Jet Streams', Page 137

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: Clear Air Turbulence (CAT) is most severe and most frequently encountered in which region relative to a jet stream'
options: Directly in the calm center of the jet core
On the low-pressure (colder / poleward) side near or below the jet axis where vertical and horizontal wind shear is greatest
Far away from all frontal zones and tropopause folds
Only at altitudes below 10,000 ft AMSL
explanation: CAT occurs predominantly in regions of strong horizontal and vertical wind shear just below the tropopause, especially on the colder, poleward (left in Northern Hemisphere) side of the jet stream core.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 16 'Clear Air Turbulence', Page 143

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In the mature stage of a Tropical Cyclone, the central calm region of light winds and descending air is termed the:
explanation: The Eye is the central region of lowest surface pressure, warmest temperatures, light winds, and often clear skies caused by subsiding air. It is surrounded by the destructive Eye Wall.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 18 'Tropical Systems', Page 157

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The normal date of onset of the Southwest Monsoon over the mainland of India (Kerala coast) is:
explanation: The normal date for the onset of the Southwest Monsoon over the South Andaman Sea is 20 May, and over the mainland coast of Kerala is 01 June.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 19 'Climatology of India', Page 171

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: During a 'Break in Monsoon', the axis of the monsoon trough shifts towards:
options: The foot hills of the Himalayas
explanation: During a break in monsoon, the monsoon trough shifts northwards close to the Himalayan foothills, causing heavy floods in Assam and sub-Himalayan Bengal while the plains of India experience dry spells.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 19 'Climatology of India', Page 172

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In a METAR weather report, the term CAVOK indicates that simultaneously:
options: Visibility >= 10 km, no clouds below 1500 m (5000 ft) or MSA, and no weather of significance
Visibility >= 5 km and sky completely clear
No clouds at all altitudes and zero wind
explanation: CAVOK (Ceiling And Visibility OK) requires: visibility 10 km or more; no cloud below 1500 m (5000 ft) or highest minimum sector altitude (whichever is greater), no CB/TCU; and no significant weather.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 25 'METAR SPECI', Page 219

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: A TREND landing forecast appended to a METAR or SPECI has a validity period of:
explanation: A TREND forecast consists of a concise statement of expected significant changes appended to a METAR or SPECI and is valid for 2 hours from the time of the report.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 25 'METAR SPECI', Page 223

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In a TAF report, the change indicator 'TEMPO 1215' means that the described weather changes are expected to:
options: Start permanently at 12:00 UTC and continue through 15:00 UTC
Occur temporarily between 12:00 UTC and 15:00 UTC, lasting less than 1 hour in each instance
Be valid only for 12 to 15 minutes
explanation: TEMPO denotes temporary fluctuations lasting less than one hour in each instance and in aggregate covering less than half of the indicated period (from 12:00 to 15:00 UTC).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 26 'Aviation Weather Forecasts TAF', Page 224, 231

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: In a METAR, 'R27/1200D' in the runway visual range group indicates:
options: Runway 27 RVR is 1200 ft with downward slope
Runway 27 RVR is 1200 metres with a downward (decreasing) tendency
Runway 27 RVR is 1200 metres during daytime
Runway 27 RVR is between 1200 and 1500 m
explanation: In the RVR group RD_R/V_RV_RV_RV_R i: R27 indicates Runway 27, 1200 indicates 1200 metres, and the tendency letter 'D' indicates decreasing over the past 10 minutes ('U' = increasing, 'N' = no change).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 25 'METAR SPECI', Page 221

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: A SIGMET is issued by a Meteorological Watch Office (MWO) to warn pilots of:
options: En-route weather phenomena that may affect the safety of all aircraft operations
Only local airport surface wind gusts
Flight delays caused by air traffic congestion
explanation: SIGMET messages give concise information concerning the occurrence or expected occurrence of specified en-route weather phenomena which may affect the safety of aircraft operations (e.g., severe turbulence, severe icing, volcanic ash, tropical cyclones).
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 21 'Met Services', Page 192

subject: Aviation Meteorology
question: The descending branch of the Hadley Cell near latitude 30° N and 30° S is characterized by calm winds, high pressure, and world deserts. This region is known as:
explanation: The Horse Latitudes are subtropical high-pressure belts located around 30° N and 30° S, formed by subsiding air from the Hadley cell. The sinking air causes adiabatic warming, cloud dissipation, calm winds, and major arid zones.
source: I.C. Joshi Aviation Meteorology, Chapter 20 'General Circulation', Page 184

subject: Technical General
question: According to Bernoulli's principle, as airflow accelerates over the cambered upper surface of an airfoil, what happens to dynamic pressure and static pressure'
options: Dynamic pressure decreases and static pressure increases
Dynamic pressure increases and static pressure decreases
Both dynamic and static pressure increase
Both dynamic and static pressure decrease
explanation: Bernoulli's theorem states that for steady incompressible flow, total pressure (static + dynamic) remains constant. As air accelerates over the camber, dynamic pressure increases and static pressure decreases, producing lift.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 2 'Subsonic Airflow'

subject: Technical General
question: An aircraft will stall whenever which condition occurs'
options: The airspeed falls below a fixed calibrated airspeed
The critical (stalling) angle of attack is exceeded, regardless of airspeed, weight, or attitude
The engine power is reduced to idle
The aircraft enters a banked turn exceeding 45 degrees
explanation: An airfoil always stalls at the same critical angle of attack (typically 15°-18° for general aviation airfoils), regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor, or flight attitude.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 3 'The Stall'

subject: Technical General
question: Induced drag is a byproduct of lift creation caused by wingtip vortices. As airspeed increases in straight and level flight, induced drag:
options: Increases proportional to the square of airspeed
Decreases inversely proportional to the square of airspeed
explanation: Induced drag is inversely proportional to the square of airspeed (Di proportional to 1/V^2). At high speeds, angle of attack is small, wingtip vortices are weak, and induced drag is low. At low speeds, induced drag is high.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 4 'Drag'

subject: Technical General
question: In a level, coordinated 60-degree banked turn, the load factor (g) and stall speed increase by approximately what factors'
options: Load factor 1.41 g, stall speed increases by 19%
Load factor 2.0 g, stall speed increases by approximately 41%
Load factor 3.0 g, stall speed doubles (100%)
Load factor 1.5 g, stall speed increases by 25%
explanation: Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle). At 60°, n = 1/cos(60°) = 2.0 g. Stall speed in a turn Vs_turn = Vs_level * sqrt(n) = Vs * sqrt(2.0) = 1.414 * Vs (a 41% increase in stalling speed).
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 8 'Manoeuvres'

subject: Technical General
question: When flying into ground effect (within approximately one wingspan of the surface), which changes occur'
options: Induced drag increases and elevator authority is lost
Induced drag decreases, effective lift increases, and the aircraft tends to float
Parasite drag increases dramatically requiring more thrust
explanation: The proximity of the ground restricts the vertical component of airflow, reducing downwash and wingtip vortex size. Induced drag drops significantly, increasing the lift-to-drag ratio and causing the aircraft to float.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 4 'Ground Effect'

subject: Technical General
question: What is the primary aerodynamic purpose of wing dihedral (wings angled upward from root to tip)'
options: To reduce parasite drag in cruise
explanation: Dihedral provides lateral stability. When the aircraft sideslips (rolls), the lower wing has a higher effective angle of attack than the higher wing, producing a restoring rolling moment that levels the wings.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 9 'Stability'

subject: Technical General
question: In a four-stroke internal combustion aero-engine, what is the correct order of the operating strokes'
explanation: The Otto four-stroke cycle consists of: 1) Intake (fuel-air drawn in), 2) Compression (mixture compressed), 3) Power/Expansion (spark fires, burning expands), 4) Exhaust (burnt gases expelled).
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 1 'Piston Engines'

subject: Technical General
question: Aviation piston engines use dual independent ignition systems primarily consisting of:
options: A car battery and two alternators
Two engine-driven magnetos, each firing one of two spark plugs per cylinder, independent of the electrical system
A single distributor firing four spark plugs in sequence
Direct injection piezo-electric igniters powered by the busbar
explanation: Aero piston engines use two independent magnetos (left and right), each powering one spark plug per cylinder. Magnetos are engine-driven permanent-magnet generators that operate completely independent of the aircraft battery.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 3 'Ignition Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: Detonation in an aircraft piston engine is best defined as:
options: Ignition of the fuel-air charge prior to the normal spark event
An uncontrolled, explosive burning of the remaining fuel-air charge ahead of the normal flame front
Backfiring through the carburetor induction pipe due to lean mixture
Normal rapid combustion at full takeoff power
explanation: Detonation is the sudden explosive combustion of the end-gas ahead of the advancing flame front. It causes extreme cylinder head temperature and pressure spikes, potentially leading to catastrophic engine damage.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 2 'Combustion'

subject: Technical General
question: Pre-ignition differs from detonation in that pre-ignition is caused by:
options: Using fuel of too high an octane rating
An incandescent hotspot (such as glowing carbon or overheated spark plug electrode) igniting the mixture before timed spark occurs
Over-cooling the cylinder head during a descent
explanation: Pre-ignition is the ignition of the fuel-air charge before the spark plug fires, caused by a local hot spot in the cylinder (overheated spark plug tip, carbon deposit, or cracked exhaust valve).
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 2 'Combustion'

subject: Technical General
question: During a pre-flight magneto check at 1800 RPM, switching from BOTH to LEFT produces no drop in RPM. The most likely reason is:
options: The engine is running perfectly with zero magneto wear
The right magneto P-lead (ground wire) is broken/disconnected, leaving the right magneto permanently LIVE
The left magneto has failed completely
The carburetor heat is stuck in the ON position
explanation: If switching to one magneto produces no RPM drop, the P-lead on the other magneto is broken or disconnected. The other magneto remains ungrounded (hot/live) and keeps firing. This is an extreme safety hazard on the ground.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 3 'Ignition Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: Applying carburetor heat to an aircraft with an iced carburetor will initially cause:
options: An immediate increase in engine RPM and smoother running
A further drop in RPM and possible engine roughness as ice melts, followed by an RPM rise once clear
The engine to cut out permanently
The cylinder head temperature to drop to zero
explanation: When carburetor heat is applied, hot air is less dense, so the mixture richens and RPM drops slightly. As ice melts, water passes through the cylinders causing temporary roughness, before smooth operation returns at clear RPM.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 4 'Fuel and Carburetion'

subject: Technical General
question: A constant-speed propeller automatically adjusts its blade pitch to maintain a constant:
options: Engine RPM selected by the pilot via the propeller control
explanation: A constant-speed propeller uses a hydraulic governor to automatically vary the blade pitch angle, maintaining the engine RPM selected by the pilot on the blue propeller pitch lever regardless of airspeed or throttle setting.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 7 'Propellers'

subject: Technical General
question: P-factor (asymmetric propeller blade effect) causes an aircraft to yaw to the left during high angle of attack flight (such as climb) because:
options: The ascending blade takes a bigger bite of air than the descending blade
The descending blade operates at a higher effective angle of attack and produces more thrust than the ascending blade
Propeller torque rolls the left wheel down on the runway
Slipstream hits the left side of the rudder
explanation: At high angles of attack, the propeller disc is tilted relative to relative airflow. The downward-moving blade on the right has a higher forward velocity and higher angle of attack, producing more thrust than the upward blade on the left, yawing the plane left.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 7 'Propeller Effects'

subject: Technical General
question: On a multi-engine aircraft with both propellers rotating clockwise (viewed from the cockpit), the 'critical engine' is the:
options: Right engine, because its failure causes no asymmetric yaw
Left engine, because its thrust line is closer to the fuselage than the right engine's descending blade thrust line
Engine closest to the fuel tanks
Neither engine, because clockwise engines are symmetric
explanation: The descending blade on the right engine produces thrust furthest from the aircraft centerline (longer moment arm). Failure of the left engine leaves the right engine operating with maximum asymmetric yaw moment, making the left engine critical.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 10 'Multi-Engine Flight'

subject: Technical General
question: In a hydraulic system, why is mineral-based fluid (such as MIL-PRF-5606) dyed red'
options: To indicate it is corrosive to aluminum
For leak detection and to prevent accidental servicing with incompatible fluid types
To indicate it has boiled under high pressure
explanation: Aviation hydraulic fluids are color-coded to prevent catastrophic cross-contamination: MIL-H-5606 (mineral) is dyed red; Skydrol (phosphate-ester synthetic) is dyed purple/green. Mixing them destroys system packings and seals.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Systems, Chapter 1 'Hydraulics'

subject: Technical General
question: What is the purpose of an aircraft electrical circuit breaker'
options: To boost voltage when the battery is weak
To protect aircraft wiring and equipment from overheating and fire caused by excessive current (overload/short-circuit)
To convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC)
To ground the magnetos when shutting down the engine
explanation: Circuit breakers protect wiring and electrical components from carrying excessive electrical current that could cause insulation melting, electrical fires, and equipment failure. They pop open automatically when rated current is exceeded.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Systems, Chapter 4 'Electrics'

subject: Technical General
question: An aircraft alternator failure in flight is normally first indicated by:
options: A zero or negative reading on the ammeter (discharge) and an annunciator warning light
explanation: Since the ignition system runs on magnetos, the engine continues running. The ammeter shows battery discharge (or zero output), and the low-voltage/alternator-fail warning illuminates as the battery takes over electrical loads.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Systems, Chapter 4 'Electrics'

subject: Technical General
question: Which flight instrument relies on BOTH pitot (ram) pressure and static pressure to operate'
explanation: The Airspeed Indicator (ASI) measures dynamic pressure (ram pressure minus static pressure). The Altimeter and Vertical Speed Indicator connect to the static source only.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 1 'Pitot-Static Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: If the pitot tube ram pressure inlet is completely blocked by ice while the drain hole remains open, what will the Airspeed Indicator indicate'
options: It will freeze at the speed when blockage occurred
The pressure bleeds out through the drain hole, causing the ASI to drop to zero
It will over-read progressively as the aircraft climbs
explanation: If the ram air inlet is blocked while the drain hole is open, trapped pressure leaks out through the drain hole. The pressure inside the capsule drops to ambient static pressure, and the ASI indicates zero.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 1 'Pitot-Static Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: If BOTH the pitot tube ram inlet and drain hole are completely frozen shut, how will the Airspeed Indicator behave during a climb'
options: It will act like an altimeter, over-reading as the aircraft climbs into lower ambient static pressure
It will under-read as the aircraft climbs
It will read constant regardless of attitude
explanation: Trapped ram pressure remains constant in the capsule. As the aircraft climbs, ambient static pressure in the casing decreases, allowing the capsule to expand. The ASI acts like an altimeter and falsely over-reads.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 1 'Pitot-Static Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: If the static port becomes completely blocked while climbing to a higher altitude, what will the Altimeter and VSI indicate'
options: Altimeter will read zero; VSI will show maximum climb
Altimeter freezes at the altitude where blockage occurred; VSI drops to zero after pressure equalizes
Altimeter continues to read correctly; VSI over-reads
explanation: Trapped static pressure holds the altimeter aneroid capsule fixed, freezing the altimeter at the altitude of blockage. In the VSI, calibrated leak capillary equalizes pressure between capsule and case, causing the VSI to read zero.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 1 'Pitot-Static Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: The two fundamental physical properties of a spinning gyroscope that enable aircraft flight instruments are:
options: Rigidity in space (gyroscopic inertia) and precession
explanation: The two fundamental properties of a gyroscope are: 1) Rigidity in space (the rotor maintains its spin axis orientation in inertial space), and 2) Precession (an applied force results in angular motion 90° ahead in the direction of rotation).
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 2 'Gyroscopic Instruments'

subject: Technical General
question: The Attitude Indicator (Artificial Horizon) utilizes a gyro spinning in which plane to display pitch and roll'
options: Horizontal spin axis with vertical gimbals
Vertical spin axis (spinning in the horizontal plane) with freedom in two gimbals
Tilted 45 degrees to sense both yaw and roll
Fixed single gimbal aligned with the longitudinal axis
explanation: The Attitude Indicator rotor spins about a vertical axis (in the horizontal plane) supported by two gimbals, giving 3 degrees of freedom. This provides an earth-vertical reference against which aircraft pitch and roll attitudes are measured.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 2 'Gyroscopic Instruments'

subject: Technical General
question: Apparent drift (apparent wander) in a Directional Gyroscope is caused by:
options: Friction in the gimbal bearings only
The rotation of the Earth beneath the gyro spinning in space, equal to 15° per hour multiplied by sin(latitude)
Magnetic fields from electrical wires in the cockpit
Vibrations from the engine exhaust system
explanation: A Directional Gyro maintains its axis in space while the Earth rotates 15° per hour beneath it. At the poles, apparent drift is 15°/hr * sin(90°) = 15°/hr. At the equator (sin 0° = 0), apparent drift is zero.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 2 'Gyroscopic Instruments'

subject: Technical General
question: The Turn Coordinator differs from the older Turn and Slip Indicator because its gimbal is tilted approximately 30 degrees, allowing it to sense:
options: Both rate of roll and rate of yaw
Angle of bank directly in degrees
explanation: The Turn Coordinator has its gyro gimbal tilted 30° up from horizontal, enabling it to sense both roll rate and yaw rate. The older Turn and Slip Indicator had a horizontal gimbal sensing yaw rate only.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 2 'Gyroscopic Instruments'

subject: Technical General
question: What is the primary aerodynamic hazard of operating an aircraft with the Center of Gravity (CG) located aft of the approved aft limit'
options: Severely increased elevator control forces during landing flare
Decreased longitudinal static stability, violent stall characteristics, and possible inability to recover from a stall or spin
Excessive fuel consumption due to heavy nose-down trim
Decreased cruise speed due to excessive tailplane download
explanation: An aft CG reduces the tailplane arm and download requirement, drastically reducing longitudinal static stability. In extreme aft CG, the aircraft becomes dynamically unstable and may enter an unrecoverable flat spin.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 9 'Weight and Balance / Stability'

subject: Technical General
question: Operating an aircraft with the Center of Gravity (CG) at its extreme forward limit results in:
options: Higher cruise speed and lighter control forces
Higher stall speed, heavier elevator control forces, and difficulty in achieving full flare on landing
Zero induced drag in straight and level flight
explanation: A forward CG requires a larger down-load on the tailplane to balance the nose-heavy moment. The wings must produce more total lift, which increases stall speed, increases induced drag (reducing cruise speed), and demands high stick forces.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 9 'Weight and Balance / Stability'

subject: Technical General
question: Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) is defined as Indicated Airspeed (IAS) corrected for:
options: Compressibility error at high Mach numbers
explanation: CAS is IAS corrected for position error (static port location turbulence and angle of attack) and instrument mechanical errors. Flight manuals provide CAS vs IAS correction tables.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Instrumentation, Chapter 1

subject: Technical General
question: True Airspeed (TAS) equals Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) under which atmospheric conditions'
options: At any altitude as long as IAS is below 100 kt
In standard ISA conditions at mean sea level (15°C, 1013.25 hPa, 1225 g/m³)
At the absolute ceiling of the aircraft
explanation: TAS is the actual speed of the aircraft through the air mass: TAS = EAS / sqrt(relative density). At sea level in ISA, relative density = 1.0, so TAS equals EAS/CAS. At altitude, air is thinner so TAS is higher than CAS.
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight / Navigation, Chapter 'Airspeeds'

subject: Technical General
question: A pilot flying at a constant Calibrated Airspeed of 120 kt climbs from sea level to 10,000 ft in ISA. The True Airspeed (TAS) will:
options: Increase by approximately 2% per 1000 ft of altitude (reaching approx 144 kt)
explanation: Rule of thumb: TAS increases by approximately 1.5% to 2% per 1000 ft of altitude for a constant CAS. At 10,000 ft: 120 kt + (10 * 2%) = 120 * 1.20 = approx 144 kt.
source: Oxford ATPL General Navigation, Chapter 'Airspeed Conversions'

subject: Technical General
question: Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) is used by pilots of piston aircraft primarily to:
options: Set and adjust the fuel-to-air mixture for best economy or best power
Verify whether the cabin heater valve is open
Determine the exact outside air temperature
explanation: EGT measures the temperature of combustion gases exiting the cylinder. Peaking the mixture (chemically correct stoichiometric ratio) and leaning or richening relative to peak EGT allows precise fuel mixture management.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Powerplant, Chapter 4 'Mixture Control'

subject: Technical General
question: Vapor lock in an aircraft fuel system is caused by:
options: Water accumulating in the fuel tank sumps freezing at low temperatures
Fuel vaporizing prematurely in fuel lines due to high fuel temperature, low ambient pressure, or excessive suction, blocking liquid fuel flow
Microbiological fungal growth in Jet-A1 tanks
Excessive lead additives accumulating in fuel injectors
explanation: Vapor lock occurs when high temperatures and/or low atmospheric pressures cause volatile fuel components to boil inside fuel lines. The resulting vapor bubble prevents the fuel pump from delivering liquid fuel to the engine.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Systems, Chapter 3 'Fuel Systems'

subject: Technical General
question: What is the primary function of the aircraft landing gear oleo-pneumatic strut'
options: To steer the aircraft on the ground only
To absorb and dissipate landing impact shocks using compressed gas (nitrogen) and hydraulic fluid forced through an orifice
To retract the landing gear after takeoff
To cool the wheel brakes after landing
explanation: An oleo strut absorbs landing loads: compressed nitrogen acts as a spring, while hydraulic oil forced through a metering orifice provides viscous damping, dissipating kinetic energy as heat without rebounding.
source: Oxford ATPL Aircraft General Knowledge - Systems, Chapter 2 'Landing Gear'

subject: Technical General
question: Which flight control surface provides longitudinal control (pitch about the lateral axis)'
explanation: The elevator controls pitch about the lateral axis (longitudinal control). Ailerons control roll about the longitudinal axis (lateral control). The rudder controls yaw about the normal/vertical axis (directional control).
source: Oxford ATPL Principles of Flight, Chapter 6 'Flight Controls'

subject: Technical Specific
